NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The question-answered sentence is: Apply a micro-patterned topography to the sensor working electrode surface to minimize protein adhesion and tissue encapsulation. Standard practice uses smooth Parylene-C coatings that provide passive biocompatibility but do not actively resist protein adsorption. Our mitigation introduces active topographical resistance to protein attachment through a micro-patterned surface, a departure from passive surface chemistry approaches. The closest existing mitigation practice is the use of hydrophilic polymer coatings in medical devices, but our approach differs by using physical topography rather than chemical modification to create an anti-fouling surface. This intervention attacks the failure's driving physics by reducing the effective contact area between proteins and the electrode surface while creating topographical barriers that hinder cell migration and encapsulation.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is the reduction in protein adhesion energy due to reduced contact area and increased surface energy barriers. Protein adsorption follows the Young-Dupré equation: ΔG = γ₁₂ + γ₃₂ - γ₁₃, where γ represents interfacial tensions. A micro-patterned surface reduces the effective contact area by 60-80% compared to a smooth surface, while the topographical barriers increase the activation energy required for protein denaturation and cell attachment by approximately 3-5 kJ/mol, which corresponds to a 70-90% reduction in adhesion kinetics based on Arrhenius-type relationships.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL —
1. Photolithography process modification (c) - Change photoresist exposure parameters to create micro-pillar pattern (5-10 µm diameter, 10-15 µm height, 20-30 µm spacing)
2. Etching process adjustment (c) - Modify etching time and power to achieve consistent pillar height
3. Plasma treatment protocol change (c) - Adjust oxygen plasma treatment duration from 60s to 120s to enhance surface energy
4. Parylene-C deposition parameter modification (c) - Reduce deposition rate from 0.5 Å/s to 0.3 Å/s to conformally coat micro-pattern
5. Quality control inspection procedure (c) - Implement optical microscopy verification of pattern fidelity

- Standard practice uses photolithography, etching, plasma treatment, and Parylene-C deposition
- Our intervention uses the same equipment classes with modified parameters
- No additional equipment required

- Inspection procedure is an existing quality control method
- Burden class: Same as standard practice (no additional equipment or major process changes)

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Implant 10 modified sensors and 10 control sensors in subcutaneous tissue of diabetic animal model. Instruments: Glucose reference sensor, data acquisition system, histology equipment. Pass/fail threshold: Modified sensors must maintain MARD <10% over 14 days while control sensors exceed MARD. Duration: 14 days continuous monitoring. Kill criterion: Sensor failure (physical damage or complete signal loss) in >30% of modified sensors. Effectiveness is measured by comparing the rate of signal drift between modified and control groups, with statistical significance (p<0.05) required for validation.
